body_markdown:
A virtual concert can require several music permissions, even when the artist performs their own songs. To **license music** correctly, separate the live transmission from the recording, replay, promotional clips and any prerecorded audio used during the show. Each use can involve different rights, owners and contract terms.


This guide focuses on U.S. clearance, with additional territory checks for international audiences. It is written for artist teams, labels, publishers and legal departments planning livestreamed or avatar-based concerts. The central task is to build a rights package that matches what the production will actually deliver, not simply obtain a document labeled “music license.”


## Map the concert, replay and promotion separately


Before approaching rights holders, prepare a short production brief. A ticketed livestream with a seven-day replay and paid social trailers is not one use. It is a package of uses that should be disclosed and priced together.


Your brief should identify:


-


**Event format:** Live performance, prerecorded show, DJ set or interactive virtual-world experience.


-


**Distribution:** Platforms, embedded players, virtual venues and authorized channels.


-


**Audience and business model:** Territories, expected attendance, ticketing, subscriptions and sponsorship.


-


**Music inventory:** Songs, recordings, backing tracks, samples, walk-on music and intermission playlists.


-


**Afterlife:** Replay windows, downloads, highlight edits, trailers and audience clip-sharing features.


Include technical details about whether the stream is recorded, whether viewers can select songs and whether the platform retains an archive. Those details can change the rights analysis. A free show still requires clearance; charging admission is not the dividing line between licensed and unlicensed use.


## Identify the rights you need to license music


The starting point is the distinction between the musical composition and the sound recording. The[U.S. Copyright Office’s guidance on musical compositions and sound recordings](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ56a.pdf) explains why these are separate copyrighted works. Ownership of one does not establish ownership of the other.


### Composition rights: performance and synchronization


The composition is the underlying music and lyrics, generally controlled by songwriters, publishers or their administrators.


A streamed concert can implicate public-performance rights in the compositions. In the United States, performing rights organizations such as ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR administer relevant repertoire, subject to their agreements and authority. Determine whether the platform, producer or another party supplies the necessary coverage. A physical venue’s license should not be assumed to cover the webcast.


When a production records music with moving images, synchronization permission also becomes central. A concert recording, replay or edited promotional video typically needs authorization for that audiovisual use. A genuinely unfixed live transmission can raise different questions, so have counsel assess the production workflow rather than treating “no replay” as an automatic exemption.


Teams that license music for a video concert should document performance coverage and audiovisual permissions separately. Neither should be inferred from the other. The broader[guide to how modern music licenses work](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/law-license-basics-how-modern-music-licenses-actually-work) provides background on these distinctions.


### Recording rights: commercial masters and backing tracks


If the concert uses an existing recording, investigate who controls that master and what permissions the use requires. Common examples include commercial tracks in a DJ set, recorded introductions, instrumental stems and backing tracks containing elements from a released recording.


Do not assume a streaming subscription or purchased download authorizes those uses. Consumer access to a recording is different from permission to incorporate it into a production.


U.S. sound-recording performance rights also differ from composition performance rights. The statutory framework for certain digital audio transmissions is not a general-purpose clearance route for video concerts. Under[17 U.S.C. § 114](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/114) , an audiovisual transmission is excluded from the definition of a digital audio transmission.


For recordings incorporated into an audiovisual production, obtain the applicable master-use permission from an authorized licensor. Confirm that it covers edits, replay and promotional uses where needed. When you license music containing samples, ask whether those samples are cleared for the proposed use rather than assuming the original release clearance extends to your concert.


### Live performances: artist approval is only one layer


A newly performed song does not use the original commercial master merely because it recreates that recording’s arrangement. But the underlying composition still requires analysis, and the new performance creates its own contractual issues.


Review the featured artist’s recording agreement, management approvals and any restrictions affecting guest performers. Secure appropriate permissions from performers for recording, streaming, editing and promotion. Union or collective-bargaining obligations may also apply, depending on the production and participants.


For avatar-based shows, address voice, likeness and digital-replica permissions separately. Music clearance does not authorize a recognizable performer’s identity or a synthetic recreation of their voice.


An artist saying “these are my songs” is not a complete clearance record. A publisher may control the compositions, a label may hold contractual approval rights and collaborators may own shares. The practical way to license music from an artist-led production is to verify those relationships before promising distribution rights to a platform.


## Verify ownership before sending clearance requests


Build a rights ledger with one row per musical work and separate fields for each recording. Record the title, writers, ownership shares, publisher contacts, master owner and clearance status.


ISWCs and ISRCs help distinguish works and recordings, but identifiers are not proof of current licensing authority. Confirm the relevant repertoire, ownership period and territories with the proposed licensor. Catalog sales, administration changes and territorial subpublishing arrangements can affect whom you should approach.


For permissions requiring direct clearance, establish whether a counterparty can authorize the complete use or only particular shares. A publisher’s approval of its share does not necessarily resolve the remaining interests. Likewise, public-performance coverage does not automatically grant synchronization permission.


Send each licensor the same production brief and request written confirmation of its authority. Track approved, pending and declined rights separately rather than marking an entire song “cleared” after one response.


Where ownership is disputed or a response remains outstanding, retain a replacement song. A production schedule should not depend on the assumption that silence means consent. It is easier to license music reliably when the set list can still change than when the event trailer has already promised a particular performance.


## Price the full package, not just the livestream


There is no universal tariff for virtual-concert music clearance. Directly negotiated fees depend on the repertoire, bargaining position and requested scope. Performance licensing may follow separate terms or rate structures.


Ask for quotes against a defined package so competing responses are comparable.


Commercial term


What to specify


Why it affects negotiations


Live event


Event date, access model and authorized transmissions


Defines the initial exploitation


Replay


Availability period, access conditions and platforms


Adds continuing use beyond the live show


Audience and territory


Geographic availability and expected reach


Establishes the distribution scope


Promotion


Clip duration, channels, paid media and sponsor context


Can involve distinct advertising permissions


Editing


Highlights, shortened versions and other changes


Determines permitted reuse and approvals


Exclusivity


Competing uses restricted and restriction period


Can reduce the rights holder’s other opportunities


Budget composition and master permissions separately, along with performer fees and production obligations. If a quote includes minimum guarantees, revenue participation or reporting duties, model those terms as well as the upfront payment.


A useful negotiation strategy is to price optional extensions in advance. For example, agree on the cost and exercise deadline for extending a seven-day replay to thirty days. The goal is to license music for the intended release while preserving affordable options, not purchase unlimited rights that the production is unlikely to use.


## Put the scope in a workable written agreement


A useful license connects each permission to a defined use. Broad language such as “digital rights” can leave both sides uncertain about archives, advertisements and platform sublicensing.


Specify the covered compositions and recordings, authorized platforms, territories, term and permitted versions. State whether the producer may provide the rights the hosting platform requires under its distribution agreement. Do not grant broader platform rights than the music licensors have authorized.


The agreement should also address attribution, payment, reporting, approval deadlines and any restrictions on editing or association with sponsors. If a right is subject to further approval, identify the trigger and process rather than leaving it to an informal email exchange during launch week.


For rights holders, distinguish a limited event permission from authorization for a permanent concert film. For producers, define what happens if the stream fails technically: can the event be rescheduled, retransmitted or made available through a substitute replay?


Keep the executed agreement, approved brief and relevant correspondence together. A platform’s licensing questionnaire is not a substitute for permission from the necessary rights holders. Teams that license music across several agreements should reconcile them against one scope matrix so that the shortest term or narrowest territory does not get overlooked.


## Confirm platform coverage and claims handling before launch


A platform’s music arrangements may cover some activity without covering your complete concert. Ask which rights, repertoire, territories and commercial formats are included, and which remain the producer’s responsibility.


Check the current terms for ticketed events, branded productions, virtual-world experiences and archived streams. An in-app music library or creator feature should not be treated as permission to export a concert to another service.


Separately, plan for automated claims. A valid license does not guarantee that matching systems will recognize the permission before interrupting a stream. Where supported, coordinate authorized channel details, event timing and any allowlisting or claim-release process with the relevant rights administrators.


Keep an escalation contact and evidence of permission available during the event. Test using the platform’s permitted procedures, but do not treat a successful test as proof of clearance.


Promotion deserves its own review. A sponsored teaser or creator campaign may exceed the concert license, particularly when paid distribution is involved. The distinction is explained further in this guide to[music permissions for influencer campaigns](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/influencer-campaign-music-who-needs-a-license-and-when) . Plan to license music for those advertisements explicitly instead of relying on the concert’s approval.


## Example: a ticketed show with a replay and sponsor clips


Consider a hypothetical artist performing ten songs live, using a commercial recording as an introduction and offering a seven-day replay. A sponsor also wants three performance clips for paid social advertising.


The clearance review has several distinct parts. The ten compositions need appropriate public-performance coverage and any required audiovisual permissions. The introduction requires analysis of both the composition and the existing master. The live performers need agreements supporting the recording and exploitation of their performances.


The replay must fit the granted audiovisual rights, territories and availability period. The sponsor clips need permission for their specific advertising context, including the relevant composition and recording rights. Performer likeness and endorsement approvals also require attention.


If a publisher approves only the live event, that approval does not establish replay or advertising rights. If the introduction cannot be cleared, replacing it may preserve the rest of the production.


This is why a request to license music should describe deliverables individually. One song can be approved for the concert but unavailable for the trailer, and a clearance ledger should make that distinction visible before editing begins.


## Build a release gate and a post-event closeout


Before transmission, require a documented sign-off against the final set list, actual recordings used and approved distribution plan. Confirm that every necessary permission is effective and that outstanding conditions have been satisfied. Give the production team a clear instruction for substitutions and unexpected guest songs.


After the event, reconcile the performed set list with the approved inventory. Submit required usage or financial reports, pay amounts due and remove replays when their authorization expires. Check scheduled promotional posts as well as the main event page.


An audience member’s unauthorized repost is not necessarily the producer’s responsibility, but official clipping tools and encouraged sharing should be reviewed in advance. Do not promise fans unrestricted reuse that the production itself cannot authorize.


## Frequently asked questions


**Can I stream a concert of cover songs?** Potentially, but covers still involve the underlying compositions. Confirm public-performance coverage and any audiovisual permissions required by the production. Performing the song yourself avoids using the original commercial master, not the need to assess composition rights.


**Does The MLC’s blanket license cover a concert video?** No. The statutory mechanical framework in[17 U.S.C. § 115](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/115) concerns specified uses of musical works in phonorecords. It is not a synchronization license for audiovisual concert recordings. A separately released audio album requires its own rights analysis.


**Do I need permission for a short music clip?** There is no general “under thirty seconds” exemption. Duration can affect negotiations, but it does not establish permission. Fair use is fact-specific and should not be assumed for concert promotions.


**Can I license music worldwide through one agreement?** Sometimes, if the counterparty controls the necessary rights worldwide. Verify that authority for each right. Otherwise, obtain additional permissions or restrict availability to cleared territories, including for replays and official promotional distribution.


## Before announcing the event


Finalize the use map, confirm licensing authority and obtain a written clearance status for every song and recording. Keep replacement music available until approvals are complete. Have qualified counsel review unresolved rights questions before ticket sales or promotional commitments make changes difficult.
